summary: Fenfluramine is a serotonergic agent now used as an antiseizure medication for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome in patients 2 years and older. It increases serotonin release and acts at multiple 5-HT receptor subtypes (and the sigma-1 receptor). Because the historical use of fenfluramine as an appetite suppressant caused cardiac valvulopathy and pulmonary arterial hypertension, it carries a BOXED WARNING for these risks and is available only through a restricted REMS program requiring baseline and periodic echocardiographic monitoring. It also causes decreased appetite and weight loss.
indications: Treatment of seizures associated with Dravet syndrome in patients 2 years of age and older
Treatment of seizures associated with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome in patients 2 years of age and older

dosage.d: Start 0.1 mg/kg twice daily (0.2 mg/kg/day); after 7 days increase to 0.2 mg/kg twice daily; after 7 more days may increase to maintenance 0.35 mg/kg twice daily
Start 0.1 mg/kg twice daily; after 7 days increase to 0.2 mg/kg twice daily (0.4 mg/kg/day)
dosage.n: Maximum 17 mg/day; stiripentol regimen lowers required dose

dosage.d: Lower starting dose and slower titration; reduced maximum (e.g., max ~13 mg/day depending on regimen)

admin: Available only through the restricted Fintepla REMS program - prescriber, pharmacy, and patient must be enrolled
Obtain a baseline echocardiogram before starting therapy
May be taken with or without food; the oral solution is measured with the provided oral syringe
Titrate per the schedule; do not stop abruptly (taper to reduce risk of increased seizure frequency and status epilepticus)
moa: The exact antiseizure mechanism is unknown, but fenfluramine and its active metabolite norfenfluramine increase synaptic serotonin by promoting release and inhibiting reuptake, and act as agonists at multiple serotonin receptor subtypes (including 5-HT1D, 5-HT2A, and 5-HT2C). Activity at the sigma-1 receptor may also contribute. Agonism at 5-HT2B receptors on heart valves and pulmonary vasculature underlies the valvulopathy and pulmonary hypertension risk seen historically.

absolute: Concomitant use with, or within 14 days of, monoamine oxidase inhibitors (risk of serotonin syndrome)
Known hypersensitivity to fenfluramine or any excipient
relative: Pre-existing valvular heart disease or pulmonary arterial hypertension
Glaucoma / conditions with increased risk of angle closure
monitor: Echocardiography for valvular heart disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension
Appetite, weight, and growth (especially in children)

preg: There are limited data on fenfluramine use in pregnant women. It should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus; untreated seizures also pose risk. A pregnancy exposure registry exists for antiseizure medications.
lact: It is not known whether fenfluramine is excreted in human milk. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother's clinical need for fenfluramine and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed infant.
renal: No dosage adjustment is needed in mild to moderate renal impairment. Fenfluramine has not been adequately studied in severe renal impairment and is not recommended in those patients.
hepatic: Hepatic impairment increases exposure; use a lower starting dose, slower titration, and a reduced maximum daily dose according to the product labeling. Use with caution.

major: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (contraindicated; serotonin syndrome) - do not use within 14 days
Other serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, tramadol, lithium, St. John's wort) - serotonin syndrome risk
Drugs known to cause valvular heart disease or pulmonary hypertension (additive risk)
moderate: Strong CYP1A2 or CYP2B6 inducers (may decrease fenfluramine exposure)
Stiripentol with clobazam and valproate (increases fenfluramine exposure - requires lower dosing)
minor: Drugs that raise gastric pH (minor effect on solution)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; no clinically significant food interaction
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - additive central nervous system depression
interactions.diagnostics: May cause false-positive amphetamine results on urine drug immunoassays

emergency: Signs of pulmonary hypertension (worsening dyspnea, fatigue, syncope, chest pain)
New cardiac murmur or heart failure symptoms

monitoring: Echocardiogram before treatment, every 6 months during treatment, and once 3 to 6 months after the final dose (valvulopathy and PAH)
Body weight and growth in pediatric patients
Signs of serotonin syndrome, especially with other serotonergic drugs
REMS program requirements and continued enrollment
counsel: This medicine is only available through a special safety (REMS) program that requires regular heart ultrasound scans
Keep all echocardiogram appointments - they check for heart valve and lung blood-pressure problems
Do not stop the medicine suddenly; stopping abruptly can cause more or prolonged seizures
Tell your doctor about all other medicines, especially antidepressants - do not use MAO inhibitors
Report shortness of breath, tiredness, fainting, swelling, or chest pain
Decreased appetite and weight loss are common - report significant changes, especially in children
pk: Seizure reduction develops over the titration period
Peak plasma concentration about 3-5 hours after an oral dose
Store the oral solution at room temperature; do not freeze; use within the specified period after opening
pearls: BOXED WARNING for cardiac valvulopathy and pulmonary arterial hypertension - the legacy of fenfluramine's appetite-suppressant 'fen-phen' era; mandatory echocardiographic surveillance and REMS enrollment
Now a recognized antiseizure medication with substantial efficacy in Dravet and Lennox-Gastaut syndromes
Concomitant stiripentol with clobazam markedly raises fenfluramine levels, so the maximum dose is lower in that regimen
Controlled substance (Schedule IV in the US) - has appetite-suppressant and CNS effects; can cause false-positive amphetamine screens
Taper rather than stop abruptly to avoid rebound seizures or status epilepticus
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered unless it is close to the next scheduled dose, in which case skip the missed dose and resume the regular twice-daily schedule. Do not take two doses at once to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: Overdose may cause exaggerated serotonergic and CNS effects including agitation, drowsiness, tremor, hyperthermia, flushing, abdominal pain, hyperventilation, dilated pupils, and serotonin syndrome; severe cases can involve seizures and cardiovascular instability. Management is supportive with cardiovascular and neurologic monitoring; treat serotonin syndrome and hyperthermia, control seizures with benzodiazepines, and consider cyproheptadine for serotonin toxicity. There is no specific antidote.
